blocks.title: 1. The Cartesian Plane and Plotting Points
teacherCues: Draw a large coordinate plane. Have students place sticky notes at given coordinates.
Ask: 'If I walk 3 blocks east and 4 blocks north, where am I? How is that like an ordered pair?'

discoveryHook.scenario: A city map uses a grid: streets run east-west and avenues run north-south. Your location is given by the intersection of Street 2 and Avenue 5. The [[kw:Cartesian plane]] works the same way—every point is defined by two directed distances: the [[def:x-coordinate|horizontal distance from the y-axis]] and the [[def:y-coordinate|vertical distance from the x-axis]].

explanation: The [[kw:Cartesian plane]] (rectangular coordinate system) is formed by two perpendicular real number lines: the $x$-axis (horizontal) and the $y$-axis (vertical).
The intersection is the [[def:origin|the point (0, 0) where the axes meet]].
The axes divide the plane into four [[kw:quadrants]]: I (both +), II ($x$ –, $y$ +), III (both –), IV ($x$ +, $y$ –).
Each point is an [[kw:ordered pair]] $(x, y)$, where $x$ is the directed distance from the $y$-axis, and $y$ is the directed distance from the $x$-axis.
[[imp: The order matters – $(3, 5)$ is very different from $(5, 3)$.]]

visuals.title: Signs of Coordinates in the Four Quadrants
visuals.caption: The sign of each coordinate determines the quadrant.

examples.title: A – Identify the quadrant
examples.prompt: In which quadrant is the point $(-4, 7)$?
steps: $x$ is negative → move left from origin.

examples.title: B – Why points on axes are not in a quadrant
examples.prompt: Explain why the point $(0, -5)$ does not belong to any quadrant.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about what it means to be on an axis.
steps: The $x$-coordinate is 0, so there is no horizontal movement.
The point lies directly on the $y$-axis.
A quadrant requires both coordinates to be nonzero.

examples.title: C – Same numbers, different order
examples.prompt: Are the points $(3, -2)$ and $(-2, 3)$ in the same location?
steps: No, they are in completely different locations.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: A common mistake is swapping the coordinates. [[imp: Always move horizontally first (the $x$-direction), then vertically (the $y$-direction).]]

questions.prompt: In which quadrant is the point $(-8, -2)$? (Roman numeral)
If a point is on the $x$-axis, its $y$-coordinate must be ___.
hints: No distance above or below the axis.

questions.prompt: Which quadrant has both $x$ and $y$ positive? (Roman numeral)

challengeCorner.prompt: A point lies on the positive $y$-axis. What must be true about its coordinates? Give an example.

blocks.title: 2. The Distance Formula
teacherCues: Remind students: the Distance Formula is just the Pythagorean Theorem $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ in disguise.
Use a 3-4-5 triangle to illustrate: from $(0,0)$ to $(3,4)$, the horizontal leg is 3, vertical leg is 4, so hypotenuse = 5.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two cities are 5 miles apart east-west and 12 miles apart north-south. The straight-line distance is NOT $5+12=17$ miles. Instead, you travel along the hypotenuse of a right triangle: $5^2 + 12^2 = c^2$, so $c = 13$ miles. The [[def:Distance Formula|formula for finding the length between two points in the coordinate plane]] generalizes this idea.

explanation: The Distance Formula gives the distance $d$ between $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$:
It comes from the Pythagorean Theorem: the horizontal difference $|x_2 - x_1|$ and vertical difference $|y_2 - y_1|$ are the legs of a right triangle, and $d$ is the hypotenuse.
Because we square the differences, the order of subtraction doesn’t matter—the result is always non-negative.
[[imp: The formula gives the exact distance; leave it as a simplified radical unless asked to approximate.]]

visuals.title: Using the Distance Formula
visuals.caption: The distance is the square root of the sum of squared differences.

formulaCard.title: Distance Formula
notes: Square each difference, add, then take the square root.
You can swap the points around and get the same distance.

examples.title: B – Why order doesn’t matter
examples.prompt: Show that switching the labels $(1,5)$ and $(4,9)$ still gives the same distance.
examples.peerPrompt: What happens when you subtract the other way around?
steps: If $(x_1, y_1) = (1,5)$ and $(x_2, y_2) = (4,9)$: $x$-diff $= 3$, squared $9$; $y$-diff $= 4$, squared $16$; same result.
The squaring removes any negative signs, so the distance is the same.

examples.title: C – Horizontal/vertical segments
steps: The $y$-coordinates are equal (2), so the segment is horizontal.
Same logic applies to vertical segments when $x$-coordinates are equal.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: Don’t add the differences directly—the Pythagorean Theorem requires squaring first. [[imp: Always square, then add, then take the square root.]]

questions.prompt: The Distance Formula comes from the ___ Theorem.
Find the distance between $(0, 0)$ and $(6, 8)$. (whole number only)
The distance between two points is 5. The horizontal difference is 3. What is the vertical difference? (number only, use Pythagorean triple: 3-4-5)

challengeCorner.prompt: Show that the points $(2, 1)$, $(4, 0)$, and $(5, 7)$ form a right triangle by computing the three side lengths and checking the Pythagorean Theorem.

blocks.title: 3. The Midpoint Formula
teacherCues: Ask: 'If two friends want to meet exactly halfway between their houses, how do you find that spot?'
Show that you average the coordinates.

discoveryHook.scenario: Two hikers are at different trail markers. To meet halfway, they each need to travel to the midpoint. The [[def:Midpoint Formula|formula that finds the point exactly halfway between two given points]] is simply the average of the $x$-coordinates and the average of the $y$-coordinates.

explanation: The midpoint of the segment joining $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$ is:
$$\text{Midpoint} = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right)$$
The $x$-coordinate of the midpoint is the average (mean) of the $x$-coordinates.
The $y$-coordinate is the average of the $y$-coordinates.
[[imp: The midpoint is always an ordered pair, not a single number.]]

visuals.title: Finding the Midpoint of $(-5, -3)$ and $(9, 3)$
visuals.caption: Midpoint = $(2, 0)$ lies exactly halfway between the two endpoints.

formulaCard.title: Midpoint Formula
notes: Think of it as the 'average point'.
Works for any two points in the plane.

examples.title: A – Find the midpoint
examples.prompt: Find the midpoint of the segment joining $(-5, -3)$ and $(9, 3)$.

examples.title: B – Why average?
examples.prompt: Explain why averaging the coordinates gives the point exactly halfway.
examples.peerPrompt: Draw a number line and place two numbers. Where is the midpoint?
steps: On a number line, the midpoint between $a$ and $b$ is $(a+b)/2$.
In the plane, we do the same for each coordinate separately.
Averaging the $x$'s gives the horizontal halfway point; averaging the $y$'s gives the vertical halfway point.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: The midpoint is an ordered pair; don’t forget to report both coordinates. [[imp: You must average both $x$ and $y$ separately.]]

questions.prompt: The $x$-coordinate of the midpoint is the ___ of the $x$-coordinates of the endpoints.
Find the midpoint of $(0, 0)$ and $(8, 6)$. Format: (x,y) without spaces.
One endpoint is $(3, 2)$ and the midpoint is $(5, 4)$. Find the other endpoint. Format: (x,y)

challengeCorner.prompt: A segment has one endpoint at $(a, b)$ and midpoint at $(m, n)$. Find the coordinates of the other endpoint in terms of $a, b, m, n$.

blocks.title: 4. Applications of Coordinate Geometry
teacherCues: Ask: 'How can we use the Distance and Midpoint Formulas in real scenarios?'
Show football pass example: a pass from one spot to another on the field.

discoveryHook.scenario: A quarterback throws a pass from the 28-yard line, 40 yards from the sideline. The receiver catches it on the 5-yard line, 20 yards from the sideline. The pass traveled about 30 yards. By modeling the field with coordinates, we use the Distance Formula to find the exact length.

explanation: Coordinate geometry models real-world situations. Place a convenient coordinate system, assign coordinates to objects, and then apply formulas.
In the football example, let the $x$-axis be the sideline and the $y$-axis be the goal line.
Throw point: $(40, 28)$; catch point: $(20, 5)$. Pass length = $\sqrt{(40-20)^2 + (28-5)^2} = \sqrt{400+529} = \sqrt{929} \approx 30$ yards.
Similarly, midpoints can represent meeting places or centers.
[[imp: The key is to choose a coordinate system that makes sense for the problem.]]

visuals.title: Football Pass Coordinates
visuals.caption: Coordinates turn a physical play into a geometry problem.

examples.title: A – How long is the pass?
examples.prompt: Quarterback throws from the 28-yard line, 40 yards from the sideline. Receiver catches on the 5-yard line, 20 yards from the sideline. How long is the pass?

examples.title: B – Why the origin doesn’t affect distances
examples.prompt: If we placed the origin at a different corner, would the pass distance change?
steps: If we shift the origin, both points' coordinates change by the same amount.
The differences $(x_2-x_1)$ and $(y_2-y_1)$ stay the same.
Therefore, the distance is independent of where we place the origin.

examples.title: C – Meeting point
examples.prompt: Two delivery drones are at $(2, 5)$ and $(8, 1)$ (in km). They need to meet at the midpoint to transfer a package. Find the meeting point.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: When modeling real-world problems, clearly label your axes. [[imp: For a football field, the $x$-axis might be the sideline, and the $y$-axis the goal line.]]

questions.prompt: To use coordinate geometry on a football field, you can place the origin at a ___ and define the axes along the field lines.
hints: Start of both yardage and sideline measurements.

questions.prompt: A pass from $(30, 25)$ to $(10, 5)$ has length $\sqrt{a}$. What is $a$? (number only)
Two cars are at $(1, 1)$ and $(9, 5)$ on a map (miles). Their meeting point is the midpoint. Find the coordinates. Format: (x,y)

challengeCorner.prompt: A ship is located at $(3, 4)$ and a lighthouse at $(15, 8)$ (miles). How far apart are they? If a rescue boat starts at the midpoint and travels directly to the ship, how far does it go?
answers: √160 ≈ 12.65 miles; midpoint to ship = about 6.32 miles
hints: Midpoint is half that distance from each, so rescue boat travels about $6.32$ miles.

blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid for Coordinate Geometry Problems
teacherCues: Use the blueprint: Understand → Solve → Conclude.
Work through a problem that combines distance, midpoint, and verifying a right triangle.

discoveryHook.scenario: Given three points: $A(2, 1)$, $B(4, 0)$, $C(5, 7)$. Use the blueprint to determine if they form a right triangle, and find the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

explanation: Apply the blueprint to coordinate geometry problems:
1. **Understand**: Identify the given points and what is asked (distance, midpoint, right triangle check).
2. **Solve**: Use the Distance Formula for side lengths; use the Midpoint Formula for centers; apply the Pythagorean Theorem to check for right angles.
3. **Conclude**: State the findings clearly (e.g., 'right triangle with right angle at B', 'midpoint of hypotenuse is ...').
This structured approach prevents skipping steps and ensures all calculations are correct.

visuals.title: Blueprint: Right Triangle Verification

rows.1: Right triangle, right angle at (4,0). Midpoint of hypotenuse is (3.5, 4).

visuals.caption: The blueprint keeps multi-step problems organized.

formulaCard.title: Coordinate Geometry Blueprint
notes: The longest side is always the hypotenuse.
Use exact radicals unless decimal approximation is requested.

examples.title: A – Full blueprint
examples.prompt: Points: $P(0, 0)$, $Q(6, 0)$, $R(3, 4)$. Is triangle PQR a right triangle? Find its area.
steps: Area = $\frac12 \times$ base $\times$ height. Base $PQ=6$, height $=4$ → area $=12$.

examples.title: B – Blueprint prevents errors
examples.prompt: Explain how the blueprint helps avoid common mistakes like mixing up the coordinates when plugging into the distance formula.
examples.peerPrompt: Think about the order of operations listed.
steps: The 'Solve' step explicitly uses the Distance Formula with substitutions shown.
It reminds you to square the differences, add, then take the square root.
The visual table format ensures you compute all three sides and compare them systematically.

examples.title: C – Practice blueprint
examples.prompt: Points: $A(1, 2)$, $B(4, 6)$, $C(7, 2)$. Verify if triangle ABC is isosceles (two equal sides). Then find the midpoint of the base.

confusionCorner.title: Watch out!
confusionCorner.body: When verifying a right triangle, compare the square of the longest side to the sum of squares of the other two. [[imp: The right angle is opposite the longest side.]]

questions.prompt: The first step of the blueprint is to ___ the problem.
For points $(0,0)$ and $(6,8)$, the distance is 10. What is the midpoint? Format: (x,y)
If three side lengths satisfy $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, what type of triangle is it? (one word)

challengeCorner.prompt: The vertices of a triangle are $(-2, 1)$, $(4, 5)$, $(4, -3)$. Find the perimeter and classify the triangle (right, isosceles, both, or neither).
answers: Perimeter = 6+2√13+2√13 = 6+4√13 ≈ 20.42; isosceles (two sides √52 each) but not right
hints: Two sides are √52, so isosceles. Check Pythagorean: $(√52)^2+(√52)^2=104$, $8^2=64$ → not right.
